subtopic: REPORT OF SPEECH DELIVERED TO ASSOCIATION OF BRITISH CHAMBERS OF COMMERCE
speechtext:
I wish to ask
the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, whether the government has taken, steps to ascertain the accuracy of a report which appears in the papers of to-day of a speech made, or purported to have been made, in England last night by the Honourable High Commissioner of Canada in London, and whether the speech has had the authority and approval of the Prime Minister or of any member of the administration. The despatch to which I refer appears, among other papers, in the Montreal Gazette of to-day, and the Gazette's report is as follows:
Ferguson Warns British Leaders
Dominions Will Outstrip Mother Country If Cooperation Lacking, He Says
(Canadian Press Cable)
London, April 23.-"Unless you are very careful how you treat us it will be only another generation before we take your place as leaders in industry and as economic leaders of the world." With these words, Hon. G. Howard Ferguson, Canadian High Commissioner to London, concluded an appeal to Great Britain to "take the dominions by the bands and negotiate with them." Mr. APRIL 24, 1931
Privilege-Mr. Stitt (Nelson)
Ferguson was speaking at the annual dinner of the Association of the British Chambers of Commerce here to-night.
He sometimes thought he declared, that owing to Great Britain's tremendous success through the centuries, when the world came to her as its financial centre and commercial leader, Britain had built up through the generations a feeling that she was more or less self-sufficient. It had not been realized that with the coming of war and destruction of the world's economic fabric, other nations had been rapidly growing in power and become powerful competitors of Britain.
"Where are you going to look for support if you do not turn to members of your own family?" he asked. "They are pressing to be permitted to sit down at the family table and work out problems on which your prosperity and happiness depend. Unless you are very careful how you treat us it will be only another generation before we take your place as leaders in industry and economic leaders of the world."
"Canada has the territory; the natural wealth and the right spirit, but we want from Great Britain to-day more capital and a helping hand. The time of depression will shorten if you will take the dominions by the hand and negotiate with them. The people of Britain and Canada want to come closer together and no government will stop them," Mr. Ferguson said.

subtopic: AGREEMENT FOR JOINT USE OF PREMISES AT REGINA

speechtext:
Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to ratify and confirm certain agreements respecting the joint use by Canadian National Railways of certain tracks and premises of Canadian Pacific Railway Company at Regina.
He said: Perhaps I should explain to the house very briefly what this bill refers to. An agreement was made in 1912 between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway for the joint use of passenger and freight facilities in the city of Regina. Later, I think in 1926, that became applicable to the different subsidiaries of the Canadian National Railways. But in 1930 the agreement was supplemented by certain sub-agreements with reference to office space and various other minor details, which changed the form of the agreement. This bill is introduced on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways to ratify that agreement, making it, as was the original agreement, for a period of ninety-nine years. Both companies desire it, and so far as I know it involves nothing of a controversial nature.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

I am a pretty hard man to listen to.
I hope the government will take into consideration the suggestions which I made last evening. The compensation act which governs Dominion employees is not fair or equitable, as I have already pointed out. The same wages and salaries are paid to all Dominion employees in like employment all over the country, but when accidents occur and they are disabled or lose their lives, then we differentiate in the treatment accorded. For instance, if a Dominion employee is injured in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, British Columbia or any of the western provinces, he receives 66| per cent of his wages up to a maximum of $2,000, or, about $111 per month. If an employee similarly employed in New Brunswick is injured-I think it is the same in Nova Scotia-he would receive 55 per cent of wages up to $1,200.

No, 66f per cent from Quebec west. The employee injured in New Brunswick would receive 55 per cent of $1,200, or $55 per month as maximum remuneration. I contend that equal treatment is not accorded to our federal employees. If a Dominion employee should be killed in any province from Quebec west his widow would receive $40 per month, while in New Brunswick she would receive only $30-I mention New Brunswick because I have some knowledge of what is done in that province-and I believe the amount paid in Nova Scotia would be $35 per month.
There are other inequalities in the act which could be referred to, but I do not desire to take up the time of the committee in discussing them. I approve of the principle of the bill and I thank the hon. minister for bringing it before the committee. However, I would reiterate that there was some difference of opinion with respect to the bill prior to the last elections, and that is one of the reasons why it was not presented. I want to take the position now as I did then, that this bill does not give equal treatment to Dominion employees or their dependents in the event of injury or death in the course of duty. I do not know of anything more discouraging or more productive of dissatisfaction than the unequal treatment of employees working for one employer, whether that be the Dominion or .provincial government or some industrial institution. It is not fair to pay the widow of a man killed in one part of the country only $30 per month, when the widow of a man killed in another part of the country receives $40, nor is it fair to pay $111 per month to one employee who has sustained injury while another receives only $55 per month. I am sure that the ingenuity of the government and especially of the Minister of Railw'ays can conceive of some amendment to this bill which would eliminate these inequalities and which could be presented before the bill passes the committee stage.

This is the same bill as was drawn up by the representatives of the different provinces in this Dominion. I explained last evening that before this bill was presented to me for presentation to the house a meeting was held in my office at which the Minister of Labour 
(Senator Robertson), representatives of Ontario and Quebec, certain officials of the different departments and myself were present. The representatives from Ontario and Quebec spoke for the whole Dominion of Canada, and they agreed to the bill as it is drawn up.
While that is all true, the fact remains that there are some inequalities existing in regard to the matters referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Keenan). The passing of this bill will add at least $70,000-that is a very rough estimate-to the cost of the administration of the act, or 15 or 20 per cent, and the government feels that it is a move in the right direction. The hon. member admits that himself. We feel that it is going sufficiently far in these times without adding further to the cost. After this bill has been in force a year or so there is no doubt that we can then consider alterations or amendments to the act, but, speaking for the government, I should prefer at the present time not to offer any amendment unless it be of a technical character.

I do not see much difficulty in that regard. As I understand the matter, the compensation assessed is really paid by the Dominion, and the provinces have not much interest in such an agreement. The point is really whether the federal employees in the various provinces are satisfied with the arrangement which is made. My hon. friend has suggested that this is somewhat similar to or perhaps textually exactly the same-I do not know-as an amendment which was suggested last year; but what has been said by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has a good deal of force, as my hon. friend has admitted, inasmuch as these employees are all federal government employes and if there should be any inequality, it can only be on account of the differences in wages or salary, because, as I understand the matter, under the compensation acts of the different provinces the compensation is based on a percentage of the wages or salary. Would it not be advisable, while my hon. friend is doing this, to make a clean job of it and fix a certain percentage of salary for all federal government employees. If the salaries are the same, there is no reason why a man in Nova Scotia should receive one amount for compensation and a man in Ontario, another? The fact that the provinces have agreed does not help very much; neither does the fact that the representatives from Quebec and Ontario have agreed help very much, because the other provinces have a different scale of compensation. I join with the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in urging the minister to consider the possibility of fixing the scale of compensation for all federal government employees on an even and uniform basis, having regard to the fact that all have a common employer.

The minister has said that he does not feel that he can accept any amendment unless something which he considers perhaps more important or more vital than the question which has been raised is brought to his attention. I just want to mention one or two matters which have been discussed already, and to point out to my hon. friend for his consideration either now or later on, when he comes to find out whether or not the trial of which he speaks has been successful, that the inequalities which he suggests exists to-day by reason of the -fact that we have all over this Dominion those who are employed by the federal government and who are paid rates of wages fixed without referene-c to the conditions in the provinces. That is

Government Employees Compensation
fundamental; you have a different employer, as I said before. My hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough suggests that you cannot have a man employed by the Dominion government receiving one rate of compensation while the employee of a civilian employer receives another rate. We have that condition to-day; for example almost every Dominion government employee is entitled to superannuation, while the civilian employee does not receive that advantage. Almost every Dominion employee is entitled to a statutory increase in salary, which is not the case with a civilian employee. Almost every Dominion employee is entitled to holidays regularly, which is not the case with a civilian employee. They are working side by side, perhaps in the same town, but that inequality exists already by reason of the fact that they have different employers.
Further than that, you already have inequality in connection with workmen's compensation. Until very lately Prince Edward Island has no provision for compensation to employees of private employers. But for some years the act we are now amending has provided for compensation in Prince Edward Island to employees of the government, notwithstanding the fact that there is no such compensation to civilian employees. So the inequality does exist, I suggest, and I suggest that where we pay our employees at a level rate of wages all over the Dominion, the compensation should be at a level rate also.
I have listened carefully to what has been said, and I feel that to some extent at least it seems as if the views expressed depend on where the speakers happen to be living. The very fact that all these people are employed by the federal government would seem to indicate that there should be uniformity and not inequality as to their compensation. I may say further that while the workmen's compensation boards are used as the machines through which this compensation is disbursed, every dollar of that compensation is paid to the workmen's compensation boards by the federal government through the Minister of Finance, and my hon. friend is in charge of this bill at the moment because his own department is really the one charged with the administration of this act, and is the conduit pipe, if I may use that expression with deference, through which these cases are presented to the various boards. The provincial boards are only tribunals after all, set up for the purpose of administering the act, and I submit it does not make any difference whatever that it happens to be a local workmen's compensation board which is doing the work, because as a matter of fact it is acting as an agent of the Dominion government.
May I say further that I do not think we are peihaps altogether seized of the fact that what is being done is not something entirely new. I quite agree that it is an improvement on the condition which existed formerly, but for years, ever since this act, which is now being amended, was passed, we have had a compensation aot for employees of the federal government. All we are doing now is to say that a certain class of these employees who were not receiving compensation before, because the words "under similar circumstances" contained in the old act did not apply in certain cases, shall receive compensation now. There are certain positions under the federal government which have no counterpart or corresponding employment in civilian life, and all we are doing by this act is to pick up these odd cases and put them on the same basis as the others. My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River suggests that while we are doing that, without making any change in the resolution brought down previously, we might go a step further. He suggests that the government should not simply rely on what its predecessors did but at the same time should provide for a rate of compensation which will be uniform to all Dominion government employees throughout Canada.
I submit these observations to my hon. friend, notwithstanding his attitude regarding no amendments. This matter of trial is really not very impressive. We know exactly what the issue is; we know just as well today as we shall know two years hence what will happen. The question is whether federal employees will be paid a uniform percentage throughout Canada or whether the rates will be different in the different provinces. The reasons which the hon. member (Mr. Heenan) has given are, I think, impressive and might well be considered with a view to making a complete cleanup of the situation. I think the principle he has laid down should be accepted.

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the Canada Evidence Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
{Mr. Guthrie.]
On section 1-Proof of entries in Dominion books.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROOF OF FAILURE TO TAKE OUT LICENCE REQUIRED BY LAW
speechtext:
The object of this bill
is to amend and to extend the operation of section 26 of the Canada Evidence Act. Section 26 now provides:
A copy of any entry in any book kept in any office or department of the government of Canada .... shall be received as evidence of such entry, and of the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded, if it is proved by the oath or affidavit of an officer of such department-
-that that record is so entered. All that is required is the affidavit of the proper person. The proposal is to amend that, in order to supply a sort of negative proof whereby the negative can be proved as well as the affirmative. A difficulty has arisen in this way :	Many departments of the government issue licences, and those licences extend throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Cases arise where persons are carrying on various activities without the proper licence; that is the charge. We can prove the fact of a licence by the affidavit of an officer of the department based on the records in the books of the department, but we are not able to prove that the party charged has no licence unless we send the book and the officer to the court to give evidence at the trial. We have a very large number of cases where the charge is that radios are operated without licence. It is a very expensive and a very difficult thing to have officers of the government travelling from one end of Canada to the other to produce books and prove that the party charged has no licence. Now, it is proposed by this section to allow the officer of the department in charge of the books of the department to make an affidavit that the party charged has no licence according to the records of the department, and that affidavit shall be received in the court only as prima facie evidence of the fact; it can be rebutted; but it is prima facie evidence that the man charged has not a licence. That is all that is sought by this amendment. We are able to prove the licence now by an affidavit, and we desire to prove the fact that there is no licence through a similar affidavit, and thereby save a great deal of expense to the country and a great deal of trouble to the officials.

subtopic: PROOF OF FAILURE TO TAKE OUT LICENCE REQUIRED BY LAW

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION- BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OR OTHER MEMBER OP GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I see the
same omission in regard to this bill; the explanatory note has been omitted for some reason, and I shall call the attention of the official in charge of these matters to the omission.
This is a very simple amendment. Under the Ticket of Leave Act, section 2, it is provided :
It shall be the duty of the Minister of Justice to advise the Governor General upon all matters connected with or affecting the administration of this act.
For a good many years in practice this work has been done very largely by the Solicitor General. During the war while the War Measures Act was in force, and while I happened to be Solicitor General, an order in council was passed under the authority of
that act, transferring the administration of the Ticket of Leave Act to the Solicitor General. In 1920, I think it was, the War Measures Act came to an end. The practice has been continued more or less to allow the Solicitor General to make recommendations in regard to the cases coming under the Ticket of Leave Act. This amendment is proposed merely for the purpose of making it definite and legal that the Solicitor General may continue to do so in future. The provision of the bill now before the committee is:
It shall be the duty of the Minister of Justice, or of such other member of the government as may be designated by the governor in council, to advise the Governor General upon all matters connected with or affecting tlie administration of this act.

speechtext:
Could not this be done
under the statute to authorize rearrangement and transfer of duties in the public service? There is a statute which authorizes the governor in council to transfer duties which devolve on one minister of the crown to another minister, and I know that so far as the late Solicitor General, Mr. Cannon, was concerned it was done by order in council under that statute, which is chapter 165 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Has my hon. friend considered that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION- BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OR OTHER MEMBER OP GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION- BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OR OTHER MEMBER OP GOVERNMENT

the officers of the Department of Justice considered it and I joined with them. The difficulty is that the Solicitor General is not a minister of the crown, he is an officer of the Department of Justice.

Quite so, and I realize

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION- BY SOLICITOR GENERAL OR OTHER MEMBER OP GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
We might have done it for the present Solicitor General, but this course was taken in order to make it clear that the duties could be transferred to any minister who happened to be a member of the government. As proposed now, any minister may be designated for the purpose. The present Solicitor General is a privy councillor; he is not what is known as a minister without portfolio, and the question has arisen as to whether he can be properly designated as a minister of the crown though he may be a member of the privy council. The privy

Salaries Act
council, of course, consists of a great many people who are not in the cabinet. The Solicitor General is in the cabinet, but in order to make the matter clear this amendment is suggested.

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 38, to amend the Salaries Act.

On section 1-Salary of Solicitor General.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY OF SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Last evening the Minister of Justice drew attention to the fact that the previous administration had, by naming him in the estimates, voted an additional amount for the Solicitor General in order to bring his salary up to the figure now suggested in this amendment. I mentioned at the time that the previous administration had sought to reduce the number of portfolios rather than to increase them, and I was going to direct the attention of my hon. friend and also that of the Prime Minister, to the fact that one reason amongst others the amount was voted in that way by the previous administration was to avoid the necessity of creating an additional portfolio.
It was contemplated that the then Solicitor General would, in due course be given a portfolio in the administration, and it was the intention of the then administration at a convenient date to combine the offices of

Solicitor General and Minister of Justice. It was felt that so long as the Solicitor General was in the cabinet as a member of the Privy Council he should receive the same salary as a cabinet minister, but it was not contemplated to perpetuate the office of Solicitor General as a separate ministerial office in the cabinet.
I mention the matter at the moment because this would seem to be an opportune time for some reduction in the number of ministers. I should be very sorry to see the position of the present Solicitor General affected in any way, but by continuing the former method of making payment of the difference in salary the government would not be committing itself as it seems to me it now is to increasing the number of portfolios but would leave the way open at an appropriate time to a reduction, in the manner indicated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY OF SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
There may be great force in what the right hon. leader of the opposition has just said, but I have a very distinct recollection of what happened when the salary of the previous Solicitor General was increased and I think my right hon. friend will remember it if I recall it to his memory. He consulted me at the time; I happened to be leader of the opposition during 1927, and he pointed out to me that the Solicitor General was going to take a great many government briefs in the supreme court and before the privy council, which would entail an enormous amount of work and save the country an enormous amount of money. I agreed, and there was not a thought or suggestion of anything else in my mind. I approved of the proposal, and I know the former Solicitor General did a tremendous amount of work-in the courts and saved the country a very large sum of money. I assume the present Solicitor General will do the same thing.
That was the only reason put to me when the increase was made. I cannot add anything to what was said by the right hon. Prime Minister last night in reply to my right hon. friend with regard to the number of cabinet portfolios. I think there is a great deal to be said in favour of a reduction, but it is not the easiest thing to bring about and I do not know that I am in a position usefully to discuss the question. It is a matter for the Prime Minister himself to consider. What my right hon. friend has said just now certainly will be brought to the attention of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY OF SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The former Solicitor
General was made a member of the government a couple of years, I believe, after he was appointed Solicitor General, and it was

Salaries Act
only after he became a member of the government that his salary was increased to the amount which is paid all the other members of the government, and I think properly so. The same thing would apply to the present Solicitor General, who also has been made a member of the government, and my pride certainly would not be great if the minister who represents the district of Quebec in the government was not a full member of that government. He is a full member, and as long as he has to attend all the meetings of council and act as other members of the government act, I am inclined to think he should be paid this salary.
I do think, however, that the other method was preferable. The former Solicitor General was paid the increase through an estimate every year, and I think this should be done as long as the Solicitor General is a member of the government. Under this bill, however, the Solicitor General will be paid, as such, the same ministerial salarj' received by other ministers, while he may be absolutely outside the cabinet and not have to attend meetings of council or come to Ottawa or be put to the same expense and the same loss of time as the other ministers.

speechtext:
But might
he not be of much greater use?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY OF SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:

Before we deal specifically with this item which has been called I should like for a few moments to discuss the matter of compiling the estimates. You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that every year the government lays on the table of the house what is known as the main estimates. This year, as usual, we have to consider a great many items contained in the blue book entitled, "Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1932". These estimates in detail will be found from page 6 to page 108 of this book. As I say, these are known as the main estimates. On page 4 of these estimates a summary is given showing the totals of the various services, to the number of forty-two. On this page are also shown the increases and decreases as they may appear in different votes. I would call the attention of the committee to a mistake which has been made, not only in these estimates but also in the estimates for past years. I am not criticizing this government any more than I am criticizing the late Liberal government or other governments which were in power before 1922. I do not know what department is responsible for the compiling of these estimates, but I think I am justified in calling the attention of the committee to the fact that the columns are not made up properly.
For instance, on page 4 there will be found a column headed "To be voted 1931-32". The second column on that page is headed "Authorized by statute 1931-32," and the third column is supposed to give the total for 1931-32. However, these are not the total estimates for the whole year but rather the total amount of main estimates as compiled and shown in the various items from page. 6 to the end of the book. The next column shows the total for 1930-1931 and is given for purposes of comparison.

But what do we find? We find not only in these estimates but in the estimates of previous years that these particular columns are not the totals of the main estimates at all; they are all the estimates for the year and consequentb", when carried out to show either increases or decreases the public is not provided with the proper information. When these estimates were tabled a few days ago by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) the. following morning the newspapers all over the country came out with the information that there was a difference in these estimates as compared with the estimates of last year amounting to 137,327,754.72. I understand why the newspapers made that mistake because they took the figures as shown in this book. However, if hon. members will glance at the book published the previous year, taking the amount of the main estimates there, shown, they will find that the main estimates were not as shown for this year, $423,722,163.35, but $399,358,101.87. I do not object to the department responsible for the publishing of these estimates showing the total estimates for the year including all supplementary estimates for the year previous and for this year, but if the comparison is to be correct, and if the public is to have the truth, then I say it is not right to show, as is shown in this book, that the estimates are some $24,000,000 more, than they should be.
What are the real facts? Instead of showing a decrease of $37,327,754, the actual decrease in the main estimates of 1932 as compared with the estimates of 1931 amounted to only $12,963,693.
I am glad the right hon. the. Prime Minister, who is also the Minister of Finance, is in his seat because I desire to ask that these estimates be compiled properly in the future. The public should be given the proper figures with regard to all the estimates.
Mr. Chairman, would it not be better to have the column headed "Total vote of 1930-31"?

No, that would not be quite fair, because, as I said, an increase or decrease, as the case may be, is shown in the other column and it is not fair to show a decrease in the main estimates by the subtracting of the main estimates of this year from the total estimates of last year. For instance, not only do these figures include, the main estimates of 1931 but they include also the supplementary estimates passed by the Liberal government before the, house dissolved last year, as well as the seven million dollars voted about three weeks ago. If the total estimates for the previous year including the supplementary estimates were shown for

This matter should be brought to the attention of the government for reference to the statistical department or whatever department compiles this blue book, so that a change can be made in the blue book for next year and the following years. speechtext:
Mr. A. E. MUNN (North Vancouver) moved the second reading of Bill No. 31 respecting the Burrard Inlet and Bridge Company.
He said:	I might, Mr. Speaker, offer an
explanation with reference to this bill. The special validating act which I have the honour to present to this house affects not only the city of Vancouver, but all the towns and municipalities tributary to the city of Vancouver; but it affects the city and district of North Vancouver perhaps more seriously than any other part of British Columbia,
Private Bills

and since I have the honour to represent North Vancouver in this house, it was thought proper that I should present the bill for ratification.
On May 4, 1910, the parliament of Canada by special act gave the Burrard Inlet Tunnel .and Bridge Company the power to build a bridge across the second narrows of Burrard Inlet, British Columbia. Under this special act the plans of a bridge were approved by order in council and by the Board of Railway Commissioners after investigation and report by a royal commission of government engineers.
After fifteen years of effort the second narrows bridge was completed in 1925 with public moneys at a cost of $2,000,000. The Dominion government contributed $269,000, the British Columbia government $120,000, and the cities of greater Vancouver and the tributary municipalities the remainder.
The Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company is owned by the city of Vancouver, the city of North Vancouver, the district of North Vancouver and the district of West Vancouver.
Between November, 1925, and September, 1930, over ten million people and four and a half million vehicles used this bridge. In 1926 the traffic between the north and south shores [DOT]of the harbour was trebled and has continued to increase each succeeding year.
The legality of the construction of the second narrows bridge was attacked in the admiralty court in September, 1928. Mr. Justice Martin gave judgment that the bridge was properly and legally constructed. Appeal was made to the exchequer court of Canada in October, 1929. The president of the exchequer court of Canada confirmed the decision of the admiralty court. A further appeal was made to the privy council in London, England, which has decided the special act of 1910 did not give sufficient power to build a bridge that in any way interferes with navigation. Therefore this privy council decision in effect says:	When the parliament
of Canada gave the power to build a bridge, it never intended a bridge to be built I
Five years of progressive development have now been cut off suddenly. It is within the power of the parliament of Canada to restore it and to stand behind the orders of the governor in council and of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the expert professional opinion of its own departmental engineers. Therefore this validating act for the second narrows bridge is now being placed before parliament this session.
The approval of parliament is asked on these grounds: First, that the bridge was built in good faith, with public money, by Cana-

dian citizens; second, that it was built with the approval of all the Canadian authorities required by law; third, that it will prevent a great waste of public moneys, and finally that it will rectify what otherwise would be a gross injustice to western Canada resulting solely from ambiguity in the wording of an act of the parliament of Canada.
A detailed history of this bridge and all facts regarding it have been sent to the Minister of Marine, the Minister of Public Works and the right hon. Prime Minister. I also have a copy which is available to each hon. member for perusal. I also had the honour to present to this house the following petition: To the Honourable
The House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada in parliament assembled
The petition of citizens of municipalities bordering on Burrard inlet in the province of British Columbia and all municipalities so bordering as signatories hereunder humbly pray:
That your honourable house may be pleased to pass an act validating the railroad and traffic bridge constructed by the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company in accordance with plans approved by the governor in council and the board of railway commissioners.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray.
Dated at the city of Vancouver in the province of British Columbia the 28th day of February, 1931.
This petition has been largely signed by the people of greater Vancouver and districts. For instance, there are the endorsements and signatures of four cities representing 300,000 people; official signatures of business firms representing 45,000 people; labour unions, associations and organizations representing 22,715 and letters of endorsement from organizations representing 2,500 people. Endorsements by the corporation of the city of Vancouver and adjoining cities and municipalities have recently been forwarded to this government. I will just refer to one, the endorsement of the West Vancouver municipal council, dated April 1, which reads as follows:
West Vancouver municipal council urge every effort be made to hasten solution of problem of Burrard inlet crossing. Loss of second narrows bridge costs municipalities interested two hundred thousand dollars per annum and personal inconvenience to five and one-half million people crossing by bridge and ferries resulting in serious loss to business connections on both
shores'	J. B. Leyland,
Reeve.
In support of this representation from the municipality of West Vancouver, I wish to quote an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Province of April 6, 1931. It says: An Appeal To Ottawa The municipal council of West Vancouver has sent an urgent telegram to the Dominion

Private Bills
government about the problem of the second narrows bridge. The council wants the government to hasten its decision, and to announce its policy at the earliest possible moment. The council recites the facts that the desuetude of the bridge has cost the north shore municipalities $200,000, and is causing daily inconvenience to the people who cross the inlet, at the rate of five and a half millions a year. We hasten to join our own appeal in this matter with that of the council's, and we are sure that therein we express the public opinion of greater Vancouver.
It is now six months or more since a log barge knocked down and sank one of the southern spans of the bridge, and put the whole structure out of commission. Since then there has been the decision of the privy council, declaring the bridge to be illegal and a menace to the navigation of the upper harbour. Since then, also, the Department of Marine has conducted its inquiry in this city, and has rendered its report to the government. We do not know what the exact loss has been to the north shore communities, but we should think the West Vancouver council's estimate of $200,000 must be moderate to the point of under-statement. As to the resulting inconvenience. it is the sober truth to say that the loss of the bridge cannot be described in those terms. It is much more than mere inconvenience for all the people of greater Vancouver; for the communities of the north shore it has proved a veritable disaster.
In the strongest possible terms, we desire to urge upon t.he Dominion government the necessity foe a decision about the inlet crossing at the earliest moment, and one helpful to the clear necessities of the case. The government's responsibility is not merely the legal one which derives from its sanction for the building of the existing structure, but it is also the practical one that nothing can be done by way of relief to the present intolerable situation except with the government's consent and help.
Ottawa is not less obligated to assist in the speedy resumption of the interrupted communications between the north and south shores of Vancouver harbour than it is to protect the navigation of the harbour. It is not too much to say that this entire community has suffered far more from the loss of the second narrows bridge in the last six months than it could possibly suffer from any probable hindrance, by reason of any bridge at all, to the navigation of the upper inlet. This is not to say that the interests of navigation should be neglected, but it is to say that the interests of communication are even more important.
I wish to call the attention of hon. members of this house to one of the many requests received from greater Vancouver, which reads as follows:
Request your consideration and support for parliamentary measure validating present second narrows bridge. Many industries north shore Burrard inlet seriously affected. Several shut down completely. Present ferry system hopelessly inadequate for industry representing sixty-two companies and several millions capital seriously handicapped in transportation to north shore. Solicit your influence in procuring speedy relief. Situation urgent. Population leaving. Unemployment aggravated.
I might say to hon. members that there is a. ferry system across Burrard inlet, connecting Vancouver city with North Vancouver, which is totally inadequate to take care of the traffic, although over $80 000 has been spent to improve it and an all-night service instituted to try to meet the situation. A few figures to show the importance of the bridge may be interesting. From 1926 to 1930, some 10,535,932 persons, 4,305,857 vehicles, 2,515 trains and 33,141 railway cars crossed the bridge. As many as 10,000 motor cars have crossed in a single day.
Traffic cannot be restored or efforts made to finance the repairs until the construction of the bridge is validated. An asset of about $2,000,000 lies idle, industries are crippled, with many shut down, and three municipalities; are financially endangered! through loss of revenue and payment of bond guarantees. Even if improvements to navigation are later required it is vital to North Vancouver and important to Vancouver that traffic be restored as speedily as possible. With proper regulations now drafted for control of shipping, a similar accident need not occur. Failure-to validate now must lead to serious unemployment. heavy loss to industry and possibly bankruptcy of the north shore municipalities. I am thoroughly familiar with the-situation, Mr. Speaker, and while there have, been some accidents in connection with the shipping I can say without fear of contradiction that if there had been proper pilots-working under proper regulations there would have been no interruptions to navigation at all. Hundreds of millions feet of logs have-been towed up the inlet, perhaps at a cost of a few cents more, but as I said before with proper pilotage and regulations these accidents need not happen. I think with the cooperation of the harbour commission, if this validating act gets through we can have those repairs carried out in a short time and the bridge put in commission so that it can be used until such time as something better can be provided.

speechtext:
Mr. ARMAND LaVERjGNE (Mont-magny) moved the second, reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the criminal code.
He said: The object of this bill, which is very brief, is to provide that in cases tried before a jury the defence shall address the jury after the crown has done so. As the law stands to-day, unless the defence brings forward no witnesses it must address the jury first. The abject of my bill is that, whether the defence produces witnesses or not, it shall speak after the crown attorney has addressed the jury. Without being in any way derogatory of British criminal practice as we have it to-day, I think it is only fair that a man should know just how to defend himself after he has heard the accusation against him. I have received letters from all parts of Canada commending the bill. I do not wish to comment unduly upon the administration of justice. As the law stands to-day, the defence addresses the jury, being followed by the crown prosecutor, and after that the judge delivers his charge. It will thus be seen that the defence has no rebuttal to offer to the address on the part of the crown attorney and the charge from the judge.
The second point in the bill is this. In his charge to the jury, I propose that the judge should be allowed to comment only upon law and not upon the facts. The jury is the master of the facts, as we all know, and there is no necessity, after the evidence has been heard, for the judge to comment upon those facts. The necessity for this amendment is demonstrated by the fact that in the province of Quebec in the last ten years about forty verdicts in criminal cases have been quashed for the reason that, in his comments to the jury, the presiding judge has gone, I will not say far, but altogether too far in discussing the facts. The theory is that if the judge comments upon the facts he shall expose both sides of the case. Unfortunately, however, it frequent^ happens that the moment a man appears in the dock, instead of being presumed innocent, he is presumed to be guilty, from the very fact of his appearance there on a criminal indictment, and he must prove himself innocent. Too often the presiding judge has forgotten to bring before the jury the facts in favour of the defence. The object of the bill, as I have said, is that the jury, having heard the evidence, shall alone consider the facts. They know them as

Criminal ( ode
well as the judge does; and an exposition of the law in the case is sufficient from the judge.
Prior to confederation the judges of the court of sessions of the peace in Quebec were permitted to preside at jury trials in the criminal assizes, and this bill is to permit a reversion to that system. Our civil judges are too busy and it is out of their province to preside at criminal trials. Civil law is different from criminal law and the judges of the sessions of the peace are deciding at all times questions of law in non-jury trials.
I have received many letters of recommendation for this bill from lawyers in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, as well as from the west and the lower provinces. My long experience in criminal work leads me to believe that this bill is necessary. I might state that the only objections against the bill have been raised by attorneys in the province of Quebec.
I trust that this information will be sufficient for the house to gain an understanding of the purposes of this bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: SUPERIOR CRIMINAL COURTS AND ORDER OF .ADDRESSES TO JURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that I am entirely opposed to this bill. It is not advisable that the judges of the sessions of the peace in the province of Quebec should be constituted superior courts with criminal jurisdiction. They have a certain criminal jurisdiction, and it is my firm conviction that their existing jurisdiction cannot be enlarged at the present time with advantage to or so as to conserve the public interest.
Section 2 of the bill would bring about a complete reversal of the procedure which has obtained in the criminal courts of England and this country from very early times. Hardships may arise under the present procedure, but I think they would be infinitely increased if that procedure were reversed. I think it is of the utmost advantage that a judge should be allowed to comment to the jury on the facts of the case. He has followed the case and he is in a position to present to the jury in clear, definite and logical sequence the facts elicited in the evidence. Within the limitations imposed by our present rules I think he should be permitted to- comment upon the facts in order that the jury may be assisted in giving the proper weight to the facts which have been adduced in evidence before them.
Mr. LaVERGNE: My hon. friend, who has a large practice, knows that within the last
ten years the decisions in nearly twenty murder trials in the province of Quebec have been quashed because of the comments on the facts made by the trial judges.

subtopic: SUPERIOR CRIMINAL COURTS AND ORDER OF .ADDRESSES TO JURY
speechtext:
I remember one case in particular where I resented the comments upon the facts which the judge made to the jury. I thought he went to the extreme in the use of most extravagant language and I bitterly resented it, and I resent it to this day; but I still think there should be no change in the procedure of permitting a logical summing up of the facts by a fair minded judge who knows the rules of evidence and who can assist the jury in determining the weight of the evidence. It is of great assistance to the jury and is a valued help in the proper administration of criminal law.
Sometimes an incomlpetent judge is appointed, but in recent years in the province of Quebec, especially in connection with the Court of King's Bench at Montreal, it has been the custom to delegate certain judges who have had experience in the administration of criminal law to preside at such trials. After all, the competent judge is a sure safeguard for the accused and he should not be deprived of any powers which he now has in directing the ordinary processes of the court. He should be permitted to give a logical summary of the facts and thus assist the jury in coming to a proper determination. I am absolutely opposed to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, as a lawyer I am entirely in favour of this bill. As explained by the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) I think it deserving of the consideration of the house. The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) objects to the bill because he claims that a judge should be allowed to summarize the facts for the- benefit of the jury. As I understand the bill, it would not prevent a judge from explaining to the jury, shall I say in a nutshell, the facts as presented to the court by the witnesses; the judge will always be allowed to do that, but he would not be permitted to comment on the facts. The twelve jurymen are there as judges and are able to come to a conclusion; if they are not, then trial by jury should exist no longer.
I believe it to be a good idea that the order of the presentation of the facts to the jury by counsel be changed. Very often the defence makes its plea to the jury and then the case is adjourned; the next day the crown prosecutor presents his case to the jury, and then follows the charge of the judge. The
Criminal Code

jury, being human, beings and not accustomed to the proceedings, are bound to obtain a wrong impression which is not fair to the accused who, as was so well stated by the hon. member for Montmagny, is innocent in the eyes of the law until proven guilty. I am entirely in favour of the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that a change so drastic as that proposed in this bill should not be made unless it is so strongly supported by public opinion as to make it almost impossible for hon. members to vote against it. For centuries almost, the administration of criminal law in the British Empire-not only in England, but in our own Dominion-has proceeded along the line now sought to be changed by the provisions of this bill. The prosecuting or crown attorney is not a partisan; he is not one whose sole object is to secure a conviction. It is well understood that the function of a crown attorney is to bring out the facts as dispassionately and clearly as he may with perfect justice to the accused as well as to the crown. The system may have broken down in individual cases, but in the vast majority of cases it stands good to-day. Under the practice as it at present exists, the accused has his chance, which is a very good one. If the crown is to be placed in the position of having last minute appeals to passion and prejudice decide the case; if the jury are to be left open to appeals that may have little to do with the facts or the law of the case, the administration of criminal law may be more likely to go wrong than it is under the present system. We might have a crown attorney who misjudged his duty, but I repeat that in the great majority of cases the administration by the crown in regard to criminal offences is marked by fairness.
As to the other point, the hon: member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne) has perhaps indicated the weakness of his own argument. He interrupted the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) to say that in some twenty cases of trials for murder in the province of Quebec, the convictions had been upset by reason of misdirection on the part of the judge. An appeal on that ground is the safeguard that obtains everywhere and a very good safeguard it is. A judge has to be very careful in his direction, not to misdirect in any respect. Appeals may be taken to the courts where they are heard promptly, and so far as my knowledge goes-not that I have had any great practice in criminal law-such appeals are invariably considered with every

regard for the interests of the accused. I cannot say that in my province we experience any miscarriage of justice by reason of the matters to which attention is called and amendment asked for in this bill. It seems to me that it would be going against the result of experience of administration of criminal law in the empire for many years to put through this proposed amendment; we would be doing it without sufficient evidence that the law should be changed, and for my part, I think that in criminal cases, as it is in civil cases, it must be of the greatest assistance to the jury to have from a judge whose business it is to know evidence and the proper way of giving it, not merely a summing up but a comment on the evidence as it is adduced. Moreover, if you have in tihe criminal code a clause such as that which is proposed in this bill, I doubt where we would ever draw the line between mentioning fact and commenting on it, and a judge in his direction to the jury, if he touches on a question of law, must invariably touch on the question of fact. If he is forbidden to eomment on tihe facts, I doubt if he could ever direct a jury so that his direction would be found satisfactory by the appeal court, although he tried most carefully to avoid anything that might be called comment. I do not know the experience of the hon. member for Montmagny, but .my observation of the administration of criminal law in British countries is that the present system works no injustice to the accused but rather gives him every chance to which he is entitled.

In the last
eight years I have had some experience in the criminal courts of Manitoba and from my limited experience I am absolutely opposed to this proposed legislation. First, if the judge trying the case is deprived of the power to analyse the evidence or to comment upon the facts, the power is taken away from the one best qualified to exercise it. If the clause becomes law, which states that the defence should always address the jury after the prosecution, the procedure will be loaded in favour of the defence. Most of my experience has been as defence counsel, and I have no complaint whatever to make of the law or procedure as it stands. As the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr Geary) has pointed out, should the bill become law we would be very likely to lose many advantages which we now have, because if a judge is not extremely careful in his analysis of the evi-

Criminal Code
deuce and in his comments upon the facts, there will be grounds for appeal. To pass legislation of this kind would be flying in the face of history and of the whole experience of English jurisprudence, and I oppose the bill.
Mr. ARMAND LaVERGNE (Montmagny):
I have had some experience in murder cases before the courts. As regards the question of appeals, the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) stated that the result would be that there would be so many appeals that the purpose of my bill would be defeated.
I must remind the hon. gentleman that appeals are expensive and it is the accused who has to pay the piper in appealing in order to have, if possible, the conviction quashed and his innocence reestablished. If the administration of justice could do away with appeals, that would be so much easier for both the crown and the accused. The hon. gentleman has spoken of the man in the box as a criminal. He is not a criminal just because he is accused; on the contrary, he is innocent until he is proven guilty.
I shall give to the house an instance which to my mind shows how necessary this bill is, but before giving it, may I say I think it is worth while to send this bill to a committee to be discussed. In the province of Quebec,
I shall not say in what city, a man was accused of poisoning his wife. The defence, for some reason or another, were not allowed to have their witnesses heard. The defence attorney decided not to address the jury. The crown attorney, in spite of the fact that the defence had not addressed the jury, decided to do so.
I pointed out to him that when the defence did not address the jury the crown generally did not do so either. The crown attorney rose, spoke for an hour and a half, and secured a verdict of guilty. The man was sentenced to death; the case went to appeal and the court of appeal decided unanimously not only that there was no necessity for granting him a new trial, but that there was no evidence against him, and they set him free. He was acquitted by the court of appeal on account of that crown attorney, who should be-and in this I agree with my hon. friend-absolutely independent and not a prosecutor, who should be there to state the facts calmly and to put them before the jury without passion, but who, being human, or prompted by an assistant attorney general, as sometimes happens in our province, is not left with that freedom of mind that we see in England. Of course under the administration of justice in England the crown attorney when he has no case will
Stand up and say that his case is not proven, because in England presumption is no evidence. The presiding judge will tell the crown attorney that his case is not proven. Unfortunately, judging by the letters which I have before me from the different provinces, it seems, on the contrary, that that seldom or never occurs in this country; in fact we seem to have reached the stage where presumption is evidence. In England, before Queen Victoria, the judge was not allowed to comment on the facts. Certainly the comment of judges on the facts is taking away from the jury the freedom to judge for themselves which they should not be denied. The facts belong to the jurors; they are the province of the jury; yet I have heard presiding judges, supposed to be independent, who would say, "Gentlemen of the jury, we are impartial in this affair," and yet proceed to comment on the facts not in exposition of the case, but rather in the way of an inquisition of the man in the box as to the most natural actions of his life which he may have forgotten, and imputing guilt to him because of his forgetfulness. I think it is about time that we should go back to the law as it was seventy-five or eighty years ago.
I ask the house to send this bill to a committee, where I can cite letters that I have received from different criminal lawyers and crown attorneys, and where we can discuss the facts and reports and judgments in Canadian criminal cases. After all, what we are looking for is justice, and if under this 'bill some guilty party should escape in the future I am quite sure it will save many an innocent person who would otherwise be condemned because the crown attorney forgot his duty or because the judge was carried away by his passion or his prejudice.

If I am not greatly mistaken, the acting leader of the government, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), when the matter was up in the house a couple of years ago, stressed from this side, in terms just as emphatic as those I am now using, the need for immediate expenditure in this very connection. I mention the point because I believe it is but fair to our colleagues from Quebec that they should feel that in all parts of Canada there is entire sympathy with them in their desire to see these historic walls kept in a state of adequate repair.

I thank my right hon. friend for his words and congratulate him on the stand he has taken. I may tell him that the Minister of Public Works, in spite of his many duties, came to Quebec to spend a few

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
days for the purpose of examining the works, the fortifications and walls and he was impressed, very much as the right hon. gentleman was. We all concur in what my right hon. friend has said.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	I would advise the
government to beware of too close an alliance with the civic authorities. We have sometimes mayors and aldermen who seem to think that these old stones should be discarded. That unfortunately is what happened in the case of Porte St. Jean. The Department of National Defence was induced to accept the opinion of the then mayor of Quebec, who was not a believer in old stone, and because his good faith was misplaced this monstrosity occurred. I understand there is an historic sites commission created by the federal government which should be consulted in matters of this kind. The city of Quebec derives a large revenue from tourists, and were this plan carried out Quebec would be a city like New York, with numbered streets instead of the old crooked ones so attractive to the tourists. These tourists are interested not only in old stone but in the Quebec Liquor Commission, but they could stop off at Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am quite satisfied that not only in this house but throughout the country there are no two opinions with regard to the propriety of doing everything possible to preserve historic sites, not only in Quebec but throughout the rest of Canada. I think it was in 1927, when I was the acting leader of the opposition, that I pledged the support of the opposition of that day to any reasonable scheme which might be brought down in this connection. I remember also in 1920 my hon. friend from Quebec-he is wrong in his dates-brought this thing very forcibly to the attention of parliament. This matter has been in abeyance a long time, but I am glad that something is to be done to preserve these historic monuments. This work will have to be continued from year to year, perhaps for all time, but the expenditure need not be very great. There are many valued sites in the city of Quebec as well as in other parts of the Dominion. There are sites in Kingston, Ontario, wdiich should be maintained, but upon which no government money has yet been spent. We on this side of the house are. just as heartily in support of a proposal of this kind as are our hon. friends opposite, and I am sure we express the view of the people of Canada as a whole.

I noticed that the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) listened most attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Montmagny, the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice. I know he is sympathetic in this matter, and I am confident he will give us the assurance that at least an amount of $50,000 will be placed in the supplementary estimates. I am sure that if he does that we on this side of the house will see that the estimate passes without objection, which is perhaps more than we can say for the rest of his items.
Having turned from the glories of war and the plains of battle to the lesser glories and perhaps more heated arguments of peace, I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works just why the different items providing for the expenditure of money in the estimates of 1930 and 1931 were not proceeded with. The first item to which I would refer is a vote of $11,000 for Cowansville. I can enumerate others, if the hon. minister so desires.

If the hon.
member has a list perhaps he had better complete it.

The next is Farnham, and
in this connection the plans must have been prepared because it was a revote last year from the year before. In this case I think the department had ample time if it so desired to have prepared all the plans, and I hardly think the minister can offer that excuse in this case.

Some time ago
there was a reconsideration of the plan; a desire for change was evinced and the matter is still under consideration.

I come now to the item
"Quebec, accommodation for military stores." An amount of $100,000 was voted for that purpose. The Minister of Public Works will doubtless recollect that that $100,000 was to be more or less of an annual grant until such time as an amount of $3,000,000 was reached, which was to provide for the construction of a new arsenal at Little River, Quebec. In the Department of Public Works there is an ordeT in council, which I have never seen but which I know is there, providing that with the removal of the Ross rifle factory, the cartridge factory and the Dominion arsenal,
there shall be expended for the replacement of those buildings at a location at Little River, an amount of $3,000,090. Originally it was intended that this money should be spent at the rate of something like $300,000 a year; but former governments, like this one, felt the need of economy and for one or two years an amount of $100,000 was inserted in the estimates of the Department of Public Works for the purpose of providing for a building for Quebec military stores, that is, I assume, for housing stores which for many years had been located in the Ross rifle factory. The Solicitor General knows very well the need was the same last year as the year before, and is perhaps greater now, because the Ross rifle buildings have been torn down. Part of the military huts which were to be demolished have been burned, and they are still as unsightly as they ever were. The arsenal is getting more obsolete, more dangerous for those who are employed therein, and the necessity for building a new arsenal is just as great as it was five years ago. Possibly it will be easier for my hon. friend and his friends to justify a military expenditure thari it would have been for hon. gentlemen leading the house at the time I was supporting a government. Under those circumstances, with a militant Prime Minister and a militant majority back of the government, perhaps the Solicitor General might look carefully into this question of expenditure to replace the Ross rifle factory.
Only this week I received a resolution which was passed by the city council of Quebec, and a copy of which was doubtless also received by the Solicitor General and the other members from Quebec city and district, calling attention to the fact that in the month of November the then Acting Prime Minister, the hon. member for Argenteuil, had, in the words of the resolution, agreed that money would be voted forthwith to proceed with the construction of a new building to replace the Ross rifle factory. Of course, since the government has changed, and long before, I have never been called, either by the present Solicitor General or by the former one, into conference with the authorities at Quebec, so that I do not know what negotiations have proceeded between the mayor of Quebec and the Solicitor General, or rather, in his absence, his deputy, the hon. member for Dorchester, or the hon. member for Argenteuil in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister. But apparently the city council of Quebec are under the impression that a. definite pledge was given. It may be all right to make pledges to the electorate and not to keep them, but it is a bad thing to make pledges to a city

Supply-Public Works-Quebec
council or other corporate body. If that promise was made, I would suggest that the Solicitor General now join with me and ask the minister to insert in the estimates a substantial amount to commence construction of an arsenal in Quebec. The Solicitor General will, I am sure, assist me in this.

All I can say to my hon. friend is that during the last three months I hare heard more about the Ross rifle factory than about any other question. I have, as a matter of fact, received a copy of the resolution passed by the city council of Quebec. Not only is the matter still under consideration, but it has been under consideration for quite a few months-
For years.
-and we are trying to reach a conclusion.

I shall not take any more promises, but will the Solcitor General insist upon his colleague, the Minister of Public Works, placing to the credit of the department for accommodation of military stores at Quebec at least an amount similar to that which has been voted in former years? At the present time I understand those stores have been placed in the immigration building Surely the Department of Public Works did not pay $100,000 to the Immigration department for the lease of its building for military stores. I am not to understand that, am I?
No.
Has any of this money been expended?
No.

If the minister will agree that the question of the Montreal postal terminals may be discussed on some other item, I do not think anybody has any objection to the estimates for the Quebec public buildings passing.
I shall be quite willing to do that.
I accept that.
